utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Before I invite the Registrar to call the case, let the record reflect that we reconvene this morning under Rule 15 bis, Judge Delvoie being absent. Yes, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Ms. Clanton; Case Manager, Thomas Laugel; and legal intern, Moritz von Normann.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I invite Mr. Stringer to resume his cross-examination, I give Mr. Hadzic the usual reminder that you're still on your oath. Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And before I begin, I have just a couple of preliminary or housekeeping matters that I wish to address with regard to Mr. Hadzic's cross-examination and its completion today. The first of those is that over the course of the cross-examination, there are some number of documents, probably five maximum, that I failed to tender into evidence after having discussed it with Mr. Hadzic. And rather than going back to those taking the time to look at the record from before and to see what was said about them, the request would be to seek the Chamber's leave to simply file a motion or to tender them by way of a written motion. We could provide all the record references to the Chamber and perhaps might be a more efficient way of dealing with that. That was the first request I had and then I also did want to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Sorry, before you move on to the second matter --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- I suppose what you have suggested would work, but would an alternative be, if, for example, during a break you and the Defence would get together and agree that the documents should be tendered to save you the exercise of doing a written motion? I don't -- I don't except that answer now but something that you and Mr. Zivanovic can consider.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. I'm happy to raise it with Mr. Zivanovic during the break and see whether we can reach some resolution on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As to the first matter, I would say that we would prefer the written motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You don't want to think about it? You may after discussion see that there is nothing to concern you. That's why I suggested that alternative.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I -- I think that there are more than one document and I'm afraid that we will not be able to see all it and to -- to -- think about all of it just during the break. But I'll try. Anyway, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I said during the break. I didn't mean during the ordinary -- necessarily during the 30-minute break. I mean, for instance, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's -- that's better option. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We could even draft the motion and provide it to counsel, Your Honour, and then depending on how that goes either we will file it or we'll present some sort of a resolution to the Chamber. Your Honour, the next item was to actually tender into evidence Exhibit 65 ter 6561 which is now given an MFI number. This was the one that I tendered last week. Mr. Zivanovic pointed out that the Defence had request from the Prosecution information about the chain of custody and where had it come from. And that information was provided to Mr. Zivanovic yesterday, and I don't know what the Defence's position on that is, but we wish to tender that at this time now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I just started to -- to write e-mail to Mr. Stringer on his inquiry. I got it this morning. We'd like to double-check, actually, whether this document was indeed provided from the Serbian government or not. This -- the document, as far as I recall, was not complete, and I'd like to -- to double-check it before I give my consent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Third item, preliminarily, Your Honour, and I don't know whether it would be necessary entirely, but I do wish to respectfully request up to an additional 30 minutes to complete the cross-examination this morning. There are a number of loose items that I'd actually like to go back to -- to clarify with Mr. Hadzic as well as a couple of ones that were always on my list. But, in any event, the request is if the Chamber would consider allowing us an additional 30 minutes this morning, which I think I would make for a total of 70 instead of where we are now at 40.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Leave was prayed, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, just a couple of quick questions and I'm going to go through a number of things that relate to matters that were already mentioned during your cross-examination or otherwise. The first couple of questions at page 9425 of the transcript, you were talking -- this was in your direct examination, I believe. You were talking about the events in Plitvice at the beginning of April, end of March 1991, when you were arrested. And you indicated that at the time you were arrested they took away your papers, some of your personal items, and that you subsequently went back to Zagreb in order to try to get those items back from the police. And you indicated that when you went back to the police in Zagreb to get those things, you went with a friend of yours. And the question is: Who is the person who accompanied you when you went back to Zagreb for those things?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a friend of mine from school, otherwise from my village, my generation, born the same year, his name is Marko Alavana.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Another question I wanted to follow up on was -- this is at page 10252 of the transcript on your cross-examination. You made reference to your secretary and your driver. This is during the period when you were president of RSK. The question here is: Who was your secretary during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was lady from Knin. Her name was Nena Sain. That's still her name. She is still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Was she -- did you have a secretary or an administrative assistant during the SBWS phase in 1991 when you were at the government offices in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a secretary in Erdut at the government there. There was just the secretary of the entire government, Mr. Pejakovic, but he acted not as my secretary but as secretary of the entire government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, one other item relates to Exhibit 65 ter 1458, which I don't think we need to bring it up. We had -- we had during the hearing -- it's a confidential FBIS document and what we've done now is to actually redact it. It was dealt with in the hearing as a confidential document in private session, and so we have now made a redacted version and we would now re-tender or we would tender 65 ter 1458 into evidence as redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Does the Defence have any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We just like to see this document because I cannot --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We can -- if the Registrar could bring it up then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objection. Sorry. No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Did I understand you, Mr. Stringer, to say re-tender? Do I understand you refer to the 65 ter number was it ever exhibited?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: No. In fact, I did not tender it at the time, Your Honour. And so when I just said re- tender, I misspoke. It wasn't tendered. It was dealt with in the hearing confidentially and we are tendering it now as redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3234, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And just for completeness, Your Honour, the Prosecution can inform the Chamber of the corresponding pages of the transcript that were in private session and if it is minded to then could make those pages now public as well since the document is public as redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. So ordered.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, just one other -- actually, not the last clarification. But one clarification regarding when you had your first meeting with Slobodan Milosevic. And because in your direct examination, this was on the 4th of July, at page 9387, your counsel, Mr. Zivanovic, asked you about having -- when did you meet Mr. Milosevic. And you mentioned that you saw Slobodan Milosevic at a short meeting with the delegation of members of the Serbian Democratic Party from all of Croatia, and that was after the TV show about the arming of Croats, the Spiegel movie. And you went on to say that this could have been a month before Plitvice, perhaps a bit more than that; is that correct? Is that your best recollection of your first time to meet Slobodan Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was the end of February 1991 but I didn't talk to him then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And the reason I ask it is because then a few days later, on the 10th of July, it came up again during your direct examination, and this is what you said. Again on when did you meet Slobodan Milosevic, you said: "I've already mentioned that before that I had one contact. Perhaps in the month of September 1991 when Professor Raskovic called me from Knin to be on this delegation of the Serb Democratic Party." And I don't know whether you misspoke there or whether this is what you intended to say or what was interpreted, but this is in the record. Now it says September 1991 and I wanted to clarify that, in fact, it was earlier as you've just indicated, in February or so?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Raskovic invited us. That was the end of February 1991. And the first time I spoke to him in my life was in September but that was over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that was the conversation you describe that was related to the negotiations in Borovo Selo with Mr. Wijnaendts?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next item, Mr. Hadzic, if we could bring up, please, Exhibit 65 ter 4869.4. Now, Mr. Hadzic, this is a still photograph that comes from the video that we looked at just, I think, on Thursday of last week; the video being P244. Do you remember us looking at this?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And there was a little bit of discussion or confusion about the name of this gentleman, and I wanted to try to clarify this a little bit. We're looking here at the television broadcast with the Cyrillic script. Can you just read what the Cyrillic script says in the photo that we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can read it. I would have made a mistake once again. Again, it's a question of perception, as they say. So this is what it says precisely: Zeljko Filipsic. It is a very unusual surname, so you assume that it is the more usual form that we know. So it is Zeljko Filipsic from Bilje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And this is more sort of a record clarification, if I may, Mr. President. I'm looking at page 10671. Because during the course of our discussion on -- on this video, Mr. Hadzic, the name Filipovic worked its way into the transcript, and actually it's indicated there that I was suggesting to you that this is someone named Filipovic. And if I said that, I misspoke, because I was intending to suggest that it was someone named Filipcic. So can we agree that in fact at least according to what we see on the image here the name attributed to this person is Filipcic?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, what is written here is Zeljko Filipsic. So I agree it is not Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The next item, Mr. Hadzic, again, this relates just to the cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see in the line 9 -- in the -- at the page 9 line 1, again, the error in -- in the last name of the witness. It is stated "Filipcic" instead "Filipsic."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, perhaps -- could you -- well, first of all, do you know the gentleman whose image we see in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could you just spell the name as it appears on the image. Just give us the letters.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Serbian you mean, in my language?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: F-i-l-i-p-s, with a diacritic which is sh, i-c with a diacritic ch. Maybe it would be easier for the interpreters if I would do it in the Latin script rather than Cyrillic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: F-i-l-i-p-s, with a diacritic, i-ch which is c with a diacritic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And before I forget, Mr. President, Your Honour, we would tender this into evidence, this 65 ter 4869.4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3235, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, last week on Thursday we were discussing two of the incidents that are referred to in the indictment. The first of which related to the disappearance of people from the Dalj Planina region, the Hungarian people, the names Pap came up during the course of that, and I actually want to clarify or correct a mistake that I made that I think was confusing to you because I didn't put it to you correctly, and so I want to correct my mistake and ask you to comment on it. We were referring also to your suspect interview that you gave to Mr. Dzuro back in 2002, and at that time, you had told him that in regard to Hungarian people living in that area, the Dalj Planina area, you knew someone whose nickname was Sabonija; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mispronounced it. The nickname is Sobonja.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in my cross-examination, I was suggesting that he was a member of the Pap family and you were disagreeing with me. And just to make it correct, this gentleman, Sobonja, was, I believe you said, the brother or he was related to someone -- a person who actually testified in this trial. And if we could briefly go into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I indicated -- I already indicated that at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that I already indicated that this part of interview was given when Mr. Hadzic was provided with Milosevic indictment and all his answers follows from the -- from Milosevic indictment. I said that I will clarify it during my re-direct. We discussed it, as far as I recall, two or three days ago or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So do I understand your position to be that you have no difficulty with the proposal, well, the application, to tender the written document for the sake of tidiness, if nothing else? And as Mr. Stringer has said, it is intended solely for impeachment purposes as a previous inconsistent statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I see again this portion of -- of the exhibit before I take the position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I was going to suggest that perhaps we could defer this application until after the break. Perhaps Mr. Zivanovic could look at it during the break and we could return to it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's fine. We're talking about two incidents here, one is referred to in paragraph 27 of the indictment. The other one relates to the Klisa, the people who came from Klisa, and that's in paragraph -- that's the incident at paragraph 29. Just -- just so Your Honour knows, in the paragraph 27 incident, Mr. Dzuro was not referring to the Milosevic indictment. He was actually reading Mr. Hadzic part of a witness statement. It was only in regard to the paragraph 29 Klisa incident in which Mr. Dzuro read or had Mr. Hadzic read part of the Milosevic indictment. And he also read a different witness statement. And so it's a little bit complicated. But, in any event, we'll provide this to counsel. We'll confer and perhaps we can reach an agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, in your direct examination on the 14th of July, you were asked about Ilok, and your counsel asked: "Did you or the government enter Ilok or go to Ilok after the Croats had moved out? Did you establish any organs of SBWS there at the time in this territory?" And your answer was: "No, we didn't establish any organs of power or authorities. We did not have physical access at the time. We couldn't reach it. There was military administration in Ilok. It was completely sealed off." Do you recall that testimony?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember when Croatians left, the military took over and occupied everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then on page 9726 again your counsel asked: "Were you in Ilok or in the rounding area when the Croats were moved out of Ilok?" And you said: "No, I wasn't either in Ilok or in the surrounding area and I did not have any information about this, any direct information, except for what I learned from the media." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, if we could please have tab -- from tab 1087. This is 65 ter 4974.06.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You were asked about Ilok and whether you went there by Mr. Dzuro, Mr. Hadzic, and I want to show you the answer you gave at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: If we could go to page 51 of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dzuro asked --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me. May we see B/C/S text, please, at the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'll give that page number just as soon as I've got it, Your Honour. I don't have it at the ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The B/C/S of this is in e-court, this document. It should be available. Perhaps we can try this. If we could try 4974.06C, the letter C. It's a shortened version. It might have the redaction on it that the Chamber indicated it wished to avoid, but it might at least move things along quickly, more -- more quickly. Looks like we're there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm looking obviously at the English, and about two-thirds of the way down the page Mr. Dzuro asks: "Back to Ilok. Did you -- did you go to Ilok after it was taken over by the JNA?" And your answer was: "I said that I passed through Ilok. So, I did go?" Vladimir Dzuro then asks: "Did you go to Ilok right after the Croats left on the 17th of October, 1991?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer, please continue. I'm having a little technical problem here but that shouldn't interfere with you're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, so Mr. Dzuro then asks: "Did you go to Ilok right after the Croats left on the 17th of October, 1991?" And again your answer: "I don't remember having gone there immediately afterwards, meaning within a period of two or three days, but maybe in a week or ten days. "I remember having met with Colonel Grahovac, who was the commander there. But it was just a courteous conversation, because Ilok was under military administration."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then we can go to the next page so that every can see that's pretty much the end of your answer on Ilok. But if we could take a quick look at page 52?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, it's a one-page document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Oh. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hadzic, actually despite what you indicated in your direct examination, you did, as you told Mr. Dzuro, go and have the ability to go down to Ilok within a week to ten days after the Croat population left there in mid-October. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct, Mr. Prosecutor. You made a mistake. And you can see that in the terminologic discussion that I had Dzuro. I said that I passed through Ilok, and according to that logic your -- the answer to your question would be yes because I passed through Ilok, but I couldn't pass through Ilok before 20th of October when Vukovar was liberated. When I went from Pacetin to Vukovar, it was only then that I could pass through Ilok. And I said that I could -- didn't do it within a short space of time. It must have been later. It must have been perhaps within 15 or 20 days. I did not finish. So it could be 15 or 20 days later but obviously it must have been more than a month. I happened to meet Colonel Grahovac by chance and we spent about a couple of minutes talking in the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender this excerpt from the suspect interview, 4974.06C.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I may have a moment, please. Yes, Mr. Stringer. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just a moment ago I was going to tender this excerpt into evidence, but I'm not going to do that actually. I've read the relevant passages from the suspect interview into the record and put those to Mr. Hadzic, and so I think that the record is sufficient on that issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can we agree that back in 2002 you told Mr. Dzuro that, in fact, it was seven to ten days, a week to ten days after the Croats left Ilok that you went down there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that. Mr. Dzuro asked me whether I had arrived in Ilok immediately after Croats left it. I said no. I said I certainly didn't do it within a couple of days. I told him that it was later and I can see now that I gave him a period of time that is certainly shorter than it -- it actually was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, just to make sure we're all able to know what it was you said to Mr. Dzuro, Mr. Hadzic, let's just play the corresponding video from the suspect interview for this part.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the interpreters, this is 4974.06C, as in Charlie. We'll wait to -- for them to let us know when they're ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We are ready.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "Vladimir Dzuro: Back to -- back to Ilok. Did you -- did you go to Ilok after it was taken over by the JNA? "Goran Hadzic: So I did not -- "Vladimir Dzuro: Did you go to Ilok right after the Croats left on the 17th of October, 1991? "Goran Hadzic: I don't remember having gone there immediately afterwards, meaning within a period of two or three days, but maybe in a week or ten days. "I remember having met with Colonel Grahovac, who was the commander there. But it was just a courteous conversation because Ilok was under military administration."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hadzic, now having seen that, does that remind you of what you said to Mr. Dzuro? You went down there seven to ten days after the 17th of October, 1991?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard seven to ten days in the interpretation. I don't know whether you are doing this on purpose or you just didn't hear me saying on the video that I went there within ten to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I hate to spend more time on this, but perhaps this time we could re-play the video, and if it's possible for the interpreters to take Mr. Hadzic's question on the video and to indicate whether the interpretation given in the interview by that interpreter is -- is correct or not because, clearly, we've got a week to seven days in -- in -- in our interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could we have the video re-played, please, with the interpretations Mr. Stringer has suggested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: "Vladimir Dzuro: Back to -- back to Ilok. Did you -- did you go to Ilok after it was taken offer by the JNA? "Goran Hadzic: I said that I did pass through Ilok. I did go. "Vladimir Dzuro: Did you go to Ilok right after the Croats left on the 17th of October, 1991? "Goran Hadzic: I don't remember that I went immediately after that. I believe that I went after 10 to 15 days. Within a period of two or three days but maybe in a week or ten days. "I remember that I met with Colonel Grahovac" --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it was an error in interpretation of interpreter who was present to the meeting, because Mr. Hadzic did not mention week. He said ten to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that I believe's what the interpreters gave us Your Honour, and so we will take that as the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you were in Ilok by early November then 1991? You had the ability to go to Ilok by early November, ten to 15 days after the 17th of October?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. I have already answered that question. Mr. Dzuro asked me and I answered from the top of my head without really thinking. I did not have anything to hide, but I said it clearly now that I answered Mr. Dzuro that I passed through Ilok. I couldn't do that before the 20th of October. I couldn't pass through Ilok because there was fighting going on for Vukovar. When I said after ten to 15 days, I should have said after a month. That was my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, again, it's page 21, line 4 -- line 3, sorry, Mr. Hadzic mentioned November, not October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you repeat your answer to Mr. Stringer's question, please, if you remember it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember. And now I'm going to repeat for the third time. In the interview I could not define the time very precisely. This is my problem. I could not pass through Ilok before the 20th of November when the passage through Vukovar became free because you have to go through Vukovar, Ilok, Backa Palanka, and then to Novi Sad. I could not pass through Ilok before the 20th of November. When Dzuro put that question to me, I provided a hasty answer. I did not know that he was implying a -- that there was a meeting of some sort there, so my answer to Mr. Dzuro's question was not really precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have P61.50, tab 111.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is an item again that -- I'm going back to your direct examination. This is a form that you testified about on your direct examination, the form that was submitted in Vukovar on the formation of the Serbian Democratic Party in August of 1990. Do you remember seeing this form on your direct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And in your direct examination, it was -- you observed that although the date of the signature there in August of 1990 is actually after the date of the form, the printed form from June of 1990, and we weren't clear whether you were suggesting that there was some problem in terms of the authenticity of this document. Are you challenging the authenticity of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is not the date of the form. It is the header of Official Gazette of Croatia at the very top of this page.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the heard it says 25 June 1990; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And on your direct examination, Mr. Hadzic, you observed that the Gazette was from June of 1990, although it had your -- the form in it from August and we weren't sure whether you were somehow contesting this form or its authenticity. So that is my question now: Do you challenge this form? Is there something irregular about it, in your view?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my best recollection, as the president of the Municipal Board, it was my duty to register in the state where I was that was Croatia within SFRY. I did it in the municipality of Vukovar, and now I really can't tell you why there is a problem with the date, why this was done in this way. In any case, this is my signature. I'm not denying that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's just take a moment and go to tab 1686 which is 65 ter 6553. I'm going suggest to you what happened here. And, Your Honour, what we're seeing in the English is - when it comes up -- is we're seeing the English translation of a blank form with 25 June 1990 in the header. And if we could go to the last page of this Gazette in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Hadzic, are we seeing -- are -- I know perhaps you don't want to say whether the B/C/S corresponds to the English that we're seeing on the screen, but let me just put it to you that what happened is that the forms for various registrations were published in the Gazette in June of 1990, the blank forms, and that what you then did was to take the blank form from June of 1990 when it was published and then simply to fill it out and submit it, then, in August of 1990, and that's why we have your signature. Isn't that how it worked back in those days?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say yes or no to that question. I told you that the signature was mine, and, as for the rest, I really don't know what to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In your cross-examination, Mr. Hadzic, we were looking at a document at tab 561, 65 ter 1278. This was an article from "Politika," page 2 of the English. This is the article, Mr. Hadzic, called: We are in favour of peace and agreement. This related to your trip to Beli Manastir on the 25th of September, 1992. Do you remember discussing this document with me? I was asking you about Mr. Borivoje Zivanovic at the time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that we mentioned Mr. Borivoje Zivanovic on several occasions; however, you would have to show me this document to jog my memory. Actually, I am looking at it, but the letters are too small. Can it be zoomed in a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me see if I can refresh your recollection. What I was asking you about were comments on your position on whether the Belgian Battalion of UN peacekeepers should be withdrawn from Beli Manastir. At page 10259 at your evidence on cross, you said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would propose that Mr. Hadzic be provided with this text to see that before he give any answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: We can go to the very end of the article entitled: We are in favour of peace and agreement. It's the very last part of it. It's referring to: "In Zivanovic's opinion even in those critical days when the return of the refugees ... was announced, the Belgians did not succeed in hiding their favour for the Croatian side." It continues. And then it says: "'We demand and we shall do it officially through our RSK government that the UN forces in Baranja pertaining to the Belgian-Luxembourg Battalion be withdrawn from Baranja,' said Zivanovic." "Hadzic agreed with that statement and promised that the government was going to officially forward the request to the competent authorities."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hadzic, on page 10259 of your cross-examination, I asked you about that. I suggested that you were with -- you were in agreement with Mr. Zivanovic on this issue of the UNPROFOR. And you said: "No, this was the journalist's comment. I said that I would pass it on to the government as far as my authority went, to send a protest because of the Belgian Battalion's conduct, but I did not want the Belgian Battalion to withdraw nor was that under my jurisdiction." Do you remember that was your answer.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. That's what happened, yes, and that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1715, Exhibit 4890.1. It's a very short video-clip. And we'll wait for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We haven't got the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you. We've got it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "The president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina, Goran Hadzic stated yesterday that he will request from UNPROFOR to pull out the Belgian-Luxembourg Battalion from Baranja because of, as he said, the battalion's improper conduct. In connection with that, the state committee for co-operation with UNPROFOR said that they are familiar with the complaints of the representatives of the Republic of Serbian Krajina about the conduct of the Belgian-Luxembourg Battalion. Relevant factors are still not able to say anything concrete about the resolution of this issue."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we now have tab 1714, please, 65 ter 4818.2.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's try it again. I don't think we're getting sound.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "We will never accept this blackmail. According to the Belgian daily "Soir," this is the reaction of the Belgian government to the demand of the president of the Serbian Republic of Krajina, Goran Hadzic, for the immediate withdrawal of Belgian Blue Helmets from Baranja to replace them with soldiers from another country. Belgium, it is stressed, has no intention of forsaking its obligations to the United Nations and dismisses the claim of the Serbian leader that members of its detachment are biased."

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hadzic, despite what you said on the cross-examination in response to my question on this, you did, in fact, yourself want the Belgian Battalion to withdraw, and you did, indeed, believe it was under your jurisdiction since you were advocating that publicly. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's not true. This was this comment regarding the meeting in Baranja and Borivoje Zivanovic's statement and now these are journalists' comments and my picture was shown. I don't remember that I wrote or explicitly asked for that because the commentary that we heard before this one, it says that the representatives of the Krajina government had asked for this, not the president. They asked for the replacement of or whatever, reexamining the influence of the Belgian Battalion. The problem was that they had heavy weaponry on their vehicles, the Belgians, and they would point them at civilians when they were patrolling villages. This caused nervousness among people, among women and children, and they were not actually guarding the border. That's how the problem escalated.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution would tender first the newspaper article, 65 ter 1278, as well as these two video-clips that we've just seen, 4818.1 -- sorry. 4890.1 and 4818.2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Any objection from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 01278 will be Exhibit P3236. 65 ter number 04890.1 will be Exhibit P3237. And 65 ter number 04818.2 will be Exhibit P3238.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, a couple of times, actually, during your evidence and also in your own statement that you gave to the Trial Chamber at the beginning, you discussed your flight, the fact that you didn't come to the Tribunal when you were indicted. And I know that you've described that and given your reasons for that in private session for the Chamber, so I'm not going to go into the reasoning that you gave, but I do want to ask you a couple of questions about your flight and the fact that you were a fugitive from the time you were indicted in 2004. And I'm going to put it to you that despite what you said it was never your intention to come voluntarily to the Tribunal, and it starts, actually, back when you testified as a Defence witness in the Dokmanovic case back in 1998. And this is 65 ter 2320, page 3118 of the Dokmanovic transcript. And it was put to you on cross-examination by the Prosecutor in that case at the top of the page here. He said: "Now, on the evening of the 27th of June, 1997, after you found out about Mr. Dokmanovic's arrest, you fled from eastern Slavonia in a boat across the Danube into Serb, didn't you? " And you denied it. And you went on to say that you crossed Erdut and went to Novi Sad. You were with your son. You denied fleeing. And, again, on line 13 the Prosecutor put to you: "Isn't it a fact that you left on the same day of Mr. Dokmanovic's arrest; correct? And you said: "That is a fact which had nothing do with it. It can have something to do with it and need not have." But on this issue of flight, Mr. Hadzic, isn't it so that even as early as 1997 when other accused linked to these events were arrested, it was then that you left Croatia immediately and moved yourself to Serbia, isn't that true, in order to avoid being arrested and being brought to the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not correct. I wouldn't want to defend this Court from you now, but how could they have arrested me because I was not indicted? So how do you get it the other way around? How can somebody be arrested first and then have a indictment issued? Going to Novi Sad and Croatia, these are completely different connotations. I didn't want to integrate into Croatia. I didn't want my children to go to a Croatian school, and I left Croatia just like many of my friends and co-workers did. However, at the time of the arrest of Dokmanovic, this culminated this reintegration and this was sort of a cross on the T, that this peaceful reintegration should be completed and that I should leave the area. I did leave the area, as I said then, in my car. I sat in the back. My son, Srecko, sat next to me. At that time he was about ten years old. He was nine years old, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dokmanovic was arrested on a secret indictment, and you didn't know if there was a secret indictment out for you as well. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could be partly true, but it is not true. I'm sorry, I repeated the Croatian word because the interpreter was speaking Croatian to me. There were some indictments against me from Croatia. They had been withdrawn in the meantime. But at that time, I didn't know and that was a difficult situation. With Croatia I have been accused of things that I did not even know about. I didn't even know what had happened. So I have been pardoned for most things in Croatia. The things that I stand accused of here are things that I do not stand accused of in Croatia because they know who is to be blamed for what.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1619, Exhibit 65 ter 6546.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And as that is coming up, Mr. Hadzic, we're going to move forward now to the 13th July, 2004. You were in Novi Sad. And on the day that the sealed indictment in your case here at the ICTY, when it was forwarded to the authorities in Serbia, that's, in fact, when you got in your car, fled, and went into hiding for the next seven years. If we go to the next page, we can see a photograph, I believe. And then the next image on the next page. That's you, isn't it, standing out in the front of your house on the day that you got in that car and fled?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take that photograph. I don't know who took the photograph. And I don't know which day this is. There's no way I can tell that it was that day. Maybe you are right, but I really don't know who took this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You did get information that you had been indicted by the ICTY and that's when you loaded the car and fled; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I received quite a bit of this information which mostly was not correct. This was probably the 30th piece of information of this kind that proved to be correct. It was sort of semi-information.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And that's when you fled and went into hiding; correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you're asking me to confirm something that is not in dispute. Everybody knows that I had fled and was a fugitive for seven years. And, as for this photograph --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, they -- interpreters did not get the end of your last answer. You were going to say something about the photograph.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying I don't know when the photograph was taken. I had the feeling, based on your question, that you were saying that this photograph was taken on the day when I fled. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Could we please have tab 1579, Exhibit 65 ter 6505.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, this is an internal memorandum that was written by Mr. Dzuro and it relates, in part, to his contact with you when he was organising -- or in contact with you about the suspect interview and making arrangements for that to happen back in 2002. And we see here under the 16th of January, 2002, he said, he wrote that: "At 1100 hours, Dzuro called Goran Hadzic on his office phone at the Nis oil company in Novi Sad. After initial explanation, Goran Hadzic agreed on a meeting on Sunday, 20 January 2002, at 1100 hours at the Park Hotel in Novi Sad." Do you remember Mr. Dzuro contacting you - I know it was a long time ago - about trying to organise this suspect interview, or meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did speak to him, but I don't know what the date was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And then if we go to the next page of the English, he then refers to the meeting taking place on the 20th of January. He says: "At 1100 hours, Dzuro and someone met Goran Hadzic in Hotel Park in Novi Sad. The meeting went" --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, counsel has an intervention so I'll stop reading it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, may we see this document unredacted?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The unredacted parts relate to other things that Mr. Dzuro was doing in connection with other investigations in other cases. We could provide it to counsel. We can provide it, I believe. I'd like to take a look at it. But it's redacted the parts that relate to other things, not Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand why not to Mr. Hadzic. But I agree if the Prosecution provide it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can continue my cross on this, we can provide an unredacted version to counsel. It's an internal memorandum. It relates to a lot of things Mr. Dzuro was doing. We could provide it to him during the break, but I would like to conclude my inquiry on this point now and also like to conclude my cross-examination before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yeah. Mr. Zivanovic, is that acceptable? Mr. Stringer continues and you could look at it during the break and see whether you have been handicapped by not having seen it beforehand?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's acceptable for me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, Dzuro writes: "The meeting went in relatively friendly mood but the lobby of the hotel was secured by some 10 to 15 body-guards. Hadzic informed Dzuro that he was armed with a pistol and that he would not hesitate to use the weapon in case somebody attempted to arrest him. Hadzic greed to be interviewed as a suspect and the interview was set for the 1st of March, 2002, at 1000 hours in Novi Sad." So, Mr. Hadzic, despite what you've said in this trial or what you've indicated, the fact is that you've never, ever intended voluntarily to come to the Tribunal. And, in fact, here you've indicated you would use force not to come. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. He was a decent gentleman. This never crossed my mind, the possibility of an arrest. I have to give a comment because the distinguished Trial Chamber may get the wrong impression. This hotel, Park, is one of the biggest hotels in Novi Sad and the owner is a person who is deceased today, Ratko Butorovic, not called Bata Kankan, a controversial businessman as they say in Serbia. I don't know why, but he had lots of security people, body-guards. They were sitting there and they also followed him in three cars wherever he went, so they sat there. I just came with my driver, whereas all of these other people were people I did not even know. They were his body-guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You informed Mr. Dzuro that you were armed with a pistol and that you would not hesitate to use it in case someone attempted to arrest you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I said that. I'm not really that thick. Dokmanovic was arrested by about 30 soldiers. That is what I heard. Although Dokmanovic was not that dangerous. I was that literate from a league and political point of view to know that some foreign policemen could not arrest me in Novi Sad. That is not serious. How can that be recorded there? It was only the police of Serbia that could have arrested me in Serbia. That would have to be clear to me. Dokmanovic was arrested in an UN protected area so it was the UN forces that arrested him. If it weren't sad, I'd find it funny. Well, I did carry a pistol around all the time, that's no secret and that's not in dispute, for my personal protection and I had a proper permit for this pistol. I never used it though, and I never even threatened anybody with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: You told Mr. Dzuro that you had the pistol with you. True?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. Why would I do that? I'm not crazy. Mr. Dzuro is a decent man, very well mannered. He did not say a single word that was bad. He was a very decent gentleman, apologised every time he would say something that might sound wrong. I mean, I would not threaten him with a pistol. On the contrary, I would protect him if anybody threatened him. He was in my town. I would be prepared to protect him in my town with his own -- with my own body. I was his host and that is sacred in our part of the world. If somebody were to attack me guest, that would be worse than attacking me or killing me. This is really not true. What you said, whether I would surrender or no, I said that in closed session and if you're interested in that, I can tell you what I think about that in closed session, if we move into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stringer. Mr. Zivanovic -- yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would start my re-direct after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to suggest that, although we're a few minutes short -- shy of the usual time, we take the break now and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, are you ready?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we start, I would address the -- the proposal of the Prosecution as to document 4974.08. In e-court, this document has 24 pages, and we are provided with a document with seven pages. So we would see that and see -- see -- seeing this documents after -- after the -- today's sitting, and the rest we will answer to tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will start by reminding you of some questions that were put to you by the Prosecutor on the first day of his examination, on the 17th of July. I'm going to read just one part -- or, rather, an assertion of his that was a part of his question on pages 9942 and 9943. The question was: [In English] "The fact is, Mr. Hadzic, that a peaceful reintegration of the SBWS, the Eastern Slavonia region that we heard about through the trial, that, in fact, could have been achieved for Western Slavonia and the Knin Krajina as well, if you, as the leader of the Serb people in Croatia, the political leader, had advocated something other than separation of the people and in order to achieve a Serbian state on the territory of Croatia. Isn't that true? A peaceful reintegration could have been achieved at any point along the way through your tenure as the leader if you had wanted that to happen. It's just that you didn't want it to happen." [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to ask you or, rather, I would like to clarify certain things. You provided your answers already. The Prosecutor, as you can see, claimed that the peaceful reintegration was what you wanted as a leader. Please tell us whether that's correct or not.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. As a matter fact, this is 100 per cent wrong. It was not up to me to have a say in that, at all. It's a thousand per mille incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what was the sentiment among the Serbs in the Knin Krajina at the time? Do you know if there was a belief among them or a conviction that they could still remain living there if the Republic of Serbian Krajina did not exist?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We just said something about 1992, whereas, the Republic of Serbian Krajina emerged only later. When I started co-operating with them, it was at the beginning of 1992. However, in the course of 1991, the sentiment was that they couldn't exist in Croatia the way Croatia proposed it and that their safety would be jeopardised. This is at least what I knew about the work of the Serbian Democratic Party. I knew that that was their position. They were not very convinced about good intentions of the bodies of Republic of Croatia, and that's why they erect the barricades, due to that fear. It's a well-known fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question may have been too broad. I'm not interested specifically in 1991 or 1992. I'm talking about the entire duration of your term of office as the president of the Republic of Serbian Krajina in 1992 and 1993. I am interested in the sentiment of the Serbian population at that time, of the population in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. Was there any concern among them about their survival there if the bodies of the Republic of Serbian Krajina stopped existing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, there were dilemmas to that effect. They did not trust Croatia, and if the Serbian bodies of government had not existed there, the people would not have stayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Again, let's go back to 1992 and 1993. According to what you learned and based on your experience and contacts that you had with the Croatian side and the international negotiators, what was your impression? Was there a desire among the Croatian authorities to keep the Serbian population in that area? I am referring to Knin Krajina, Western Slavonia, Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice that desire. I -- I don't think it existed, although there was a lot of lip service paid to that, but there was no real desire for the Serbian people to remain living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what happened to the Serbian population that lived in Croatia, the Serbian population after the Croatian forces reintegrated Western Slavonia and Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The biggest ethnic cleansing in Europe after the Second World War happened there. The Serbs almost disappeared from the area. They were like precious metal. They remained only in traces, as the chemists would put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what happened to the part of the population which did not leave which remained living in the territory of Western Slavonia and Knin Krajina after Operations Storm and Flash?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They feared very badly. They faired very badly. We all could see that. I'm sure that you know that, the Prosecution know that. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber knows about the conversations or discussions in the Brioni isles before that operation. That plan was drafted there and they said that their safety should be guaranteed only formally. But the plan was the expel all the Serbs from Croatia. Those who believed the words that were said were elderly people who actually lost their lives during the incidents. Nobody was tried for those incidents although there were some attempts to bring people to justice in Zagreb, but nothing came out of that, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I read Prosecutor's question to you a while ago. Amongst other things, it says in that question that you did not want the peaceful reintegration. You -- you wanted the peoples to be separated from each other. My question is this: When it comes to the reintegration of Knin Krajina and Western Slavonia, did it result in the separation of the peoples or not?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That reintegration of Knin Krajina and Western Slavonia was forcible. The Croatian side simply cleansed the territory and separated the Serbian people from the Croatian people. In other words, nothing of that was up to me. The Croats did it the way they did it. Unfortunately, they enjoyed support by a segment of the international community as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When if comes to Operations Storm and Flash, they took place over 20 years ago. According to what you know, have the authorities allowed the return of those Serbs who had been expelled from Knin Krajina and Western Slavonia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution is going to object to this line of questioning. It is relating to events that took place in 1995 after the relevant parts in the indictment in this case. It goes to tu quoque but probably most significantly of all, the Chamber has heard volumes of evidence and testimony throughout the trial on these issues. They're not seriously in dispute in terms of what happened to the Serbian population in these areas in 1995, for example, but we're taking up valuable court time for an issue that has been gone into in length and it's of marginal relevance to the extent it's not tu quoque at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I quote the Prosecution's question where he said that Mr. Hadzic insisted on -- sorry. On -- on -- on the separation of people -- of the people. And I just like to clarify whether the separation of people occurred, and if separation of people occurred, when it occurred and why it occurred, and -- and my last question was: Whether the separation of people still exists or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And with that, you move on. When you said your last question, you mean your last question on this topic, not nearly the last question you asked. In other words, what I'm suggesting is that -- in response to the objection raised by Mr. Stringer, that you wrap it up with that last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't ... I don't know whether Mr. Hadzic already answered something of --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not answer but I can. That separation still exists. Serbs did not return to those regions of Croatia and their numbers there are not nearly as significant as it was before those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me what happened to the houses and apartments of those people, the people who had abandoned Croatia in 1995?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those apartments were systematically confiscated, those apartments in the city. And a lot of the houses were destroyed also as part of a systematic campaign. They were either torched or blown up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor also asserted in the courtroom that you wanted to gain control over the territories where Serbs predominated by way of expelling non-Serbs. According to what you know, the houses that were abandoned by the non-Serbs between the year 1991 and 1993, were they also torched, destroyed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both what I know and the truth about it are proportionate. What I know is the truth. That is to say, that the houses were not torched or torn down. I think that it's quite opposite to what happened in Croatia with the Serbs' houses because you've heard the testimony of Mr. Dzakula and other witness who testified about the systematic destruction of as many as 184 villages in Western Slavonia. There were such incidents during 1991 and 1992 but this was a systematic campaign, both the expulsion and the destruction of houses in 1995. The example of Ilok showed the Trial Chamber that the Serbs from Western Slavonia were temporarily moved into the houses. They preserved them. They have abandoned them. And the Croats normally returned to their houses, which were preserved intact, and most of them even included and still had the furniture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, if you remember, we had an opportunity to see, inter alia, many video-clips from Vukovar and we also heard many testimonies about the circumstances in the town after the end of combat operations and you saw that it was almost completely destroyed. What I'm interested in is whether you know if, during the combat operations and otherwise, only the non-Serbs' houses were destroyed in Vukovar or not.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Vukovar was destroyed unselectively, so both the Serbs and the Croats' houses were destroyed. In my view, it was a totally stupid war and it was an unnecessary destruction of facilities and people. We concluded that, and I saw it for the first time when I came to Vukovar for the first time on the 20th of November, because it cannot be described in words how horrible that was for all of us who saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: From what you know, were the houses torn down, destroyed during the combat operations or later when the combat operations were no longer underway?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, that's the true. And everybody knows that. It only happened during the combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: One section of the cross-examination was devoted to the Vance Plan and your position regarding that plan. I will read out to you a part of the Prosecutor's question on page 10378: [In English] "You just said that we did not deal with the problem of settlement and resettlement at all. In fact, Mr. Hadzic, that's not true. You were the lead negotiator in the international negotiations taking place about the Vance Plan, and the Vance Plan and your involvement in it was all about settlement and resettlement. How can you claim that you didn't have any involvement or participation or deal with the problem of settlement and resettlement?" [Interpretation] You can see here two claims suggested by the Prosecutor. We'll begin with the first one; namely, that you were a leading negotiator in the international negotiations taking place about the Vance Plan. Can you tell us whether you, indeed, were the lead negotiator with regards to the Vance Plan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not the lead negotiator. I did have a meeting with Mr. Goulding once and with Mr. Vance once. But that was unimportant. I think that I was the last one on the list of negotiators, not that I wasn't only the lead one, but I was a completely unimportant negotiator. That is incorrect in the question and everything else that was told is also incorrect. So I can explain that when you ask me about the particulars.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us from what you know who was or who were the lead negotiators with regard to the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have a full knowledge at that time, but as it seemed to me, it was the federal state, that is to say, the SFRY. And there was also Serbia, that is to say, Slobodan Milosevic and some of his associates. I don't know who. So both Serbia and SFRY. They were held in Belgrade, and the other side was in Zagreb. So no one asked us anything. They would just let us know the information about what was going on, Mr. Vance did, but we couldn't change anything important about it. And also in the question how the things are linked, the issue of settlement and resettlement is linked with the Vance Plan. In my language it's called conflation of conclusions. When I said that I didn't have anything to do with settlement and resettlement, I meant during the time when I was the president of the region and the president of the republic, and the Vance Plan talked about the return of refugees and that was our obligation, and we wanted them to return as soon as the conditions for that were created.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll get to that topic but, first, to illuminate everything around these negotiations. When you say that you couldn't change anything, do you imply yourself personally, or do you imply the representatives of the Serbian Krajina, that is to say, SBWS?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally could not change anything, and, generally, my entire side from SBWS couldn't. We only expressed concern about the security of the people. We proposed that the UNPROFOR that was coming to keep the border should prevent Croatian raids. They didn't do it. They guaranteed security. It was not at high level of guarantee but we had to accept it because we had no choice. And my goal was to end the war. That was my goal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you in a position to influence the adjustments of the plans so that some of its provisions might be changed? Was it ever discussed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it wasn't discussed, nor could I do any such thing. The plan was accepted by Zagreb and Belgrade and the United Nations. They formally adopted it and signed it. We never even signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to your understanding of the Vance Plan, who had the obligation to implement the plan and to vouchsafe its implementation in the territory of SBWS and the Krajina, so I mean the Western Krajina and the Knin Krajina?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two stage, as far as I understood that. The first stage was before the -- the definitive taking over of the UN and the guarantees were to be provided by the SFRY, the federal state. And from that moment on, UNPROFOR guaranteed everything. And it wasn't only my view, but that's how it was, that was the agreement, the UNPROFOR took over the responsibility for the security of the entire territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have heard the Prosecutor's question in which he says -- I will repeat that part: [In English] "And the Vance Plan and your involvement in it, it was all about settlement and resettlement?" [Interpretation] Could you tell us whether that is a correct interpretation, that the whole Vance Plan boiled down to settlement and resettlement?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course this is not correct. That only had to do with the last step, and there were many preceding steps and pre-conditions for this to be fulfilled. So, of course, it's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that that was the last step, do you remember whether the Vance Plan envisaged something with regard to the security of the people living in the zones that were under the UN protection; and, if it did envisage anything, what was it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were called protected zones. The Vance Plan implied providing security to the population in these zones, so the very name included that meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did that imply all of the population or just the minority that was present there at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan, when we negotiated about it, and when it was adopted, it was quite the opposite. It didn't have to do with the minority but the majority and, of course, all the people living there. But there were negotiations because the Serbs were afraid that they wouldn't be provided with adequate protection. The Vance Plan guaranteed protection to the Serbs that Croatia wouldn't attack them and the next step was to guarantee security to all the population, including the minority and the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your contacts with international representatives, you have seen a number of documents relating to certain complaints about the protection of some ethnic minorities; in particular, the Croats who lived in the territory of the Republic of Serbian Krajina. From what you know, did these representatives in discussions with you ever express any concern about the protection of the entire population, especially protecting them in from armed attacks that were carried out across the separation lines?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never in discussion with me, even though I received only one report that in Eastern Slavonia the Russian Battalion returned fire against the Croats. They never responded. Whenever the Croats attacked, they would seek shelter, and they would allow the Croatian army to carry out these raids. That was the information I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did these international representatives ever provide any explanation in view of the contacts you had with them, explanation as to why they did not fulfil this obligation that they had to protect the border from Croatian army raids into protected zones or --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, we object to the question. We don't agree that it accurately sets out obligations in respect of the Vance Plan among peacekeepers when active military operations are underway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question was not as to the active military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, what was referred to, Your Honour, Mr. Hadzic just said whenever the Croats attacked they would seek shelter, they being the UNPROFOR. And they would allow the Croatian army to carry out these raids and then the question was: Did these international representatives ever provide any explanation in view of the contacts you had with them, explanation as to why they did not fill this obligation that they had to protect the border from the Croatian army raids. And our position is that this is not an obligation to engage in military operations or to protect the population when the Croatian army is attacking. We can disagree, perhaps agree to disagree, on what Vance provided in this respect, but it's our submission that counsel's not accurately stating what the Vance Plan provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Vance Plan provided the security of the population in UN protected areas, and it implies the protection from -- on the raids across the borders too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: To the extent that any of this is relevant at the end of the day, in terms of such decisions as the Chamber must make, may I suggest that this be reserved for your final submissions because there's some nuances which cannot, to my mind, be adequately addressed by trying to refine the question. So please continue, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. Hadzic. If you can please repeat your answer, if you still remember the question I asked you.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you'd like me to repeat the question --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not necessary. First of all, I have to say that Mr. Vance or Goulding said what I now heard from one of the parties. If they had heard that, the Serbs wouldn't have stayed, they would have moved out if they said they wouldn't guarantee security. They did guarantee security to us. But, as I already said, during the Croatian actions, they did not prevent that, and what is more, there were no sanctions for Croatia because of those violations of the Vance Plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's a bit unclear in the transcript. It's all right now. It's been corrected. I do apologise. Another question that was raised here was -- it was actually in relation to moving out, resettlement, and so on. The Prosecutor put a question to you that I'm going to read out, 10369 is the page reference: [In English] "Well, under the Vance Plan which you agreed to wasn't under the Vance Plan that, in fact, those Croats who were no longer there were to come back, return of refugees; right? That's what was supposed to -- that's -- that what was supposed to happen." [Interpretation] This is what I'm interested in. In view of the way the question was put, can you tell us, to the best of your knowledge, did the Vance Plan only pertain to the return of Croats who had left or did it pertain generally to refugees who had left their homes during the war operations, regardless of ethnic affiliation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my understanding, the Vance Plan pertained to all persons, all refugees, irrespective of ethnicity. Had it been any different, there would have been no point in discussing it. It would have meant discrimination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, on the basis of contacts with international representatives, precisely in respect of this topic, did you get the impression that they equally cared about the return of Croat refugees to the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the return of Serb refugees to Croatia or, rather, those parts that were already under the control of the Croatian armed forces?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not equally. You asked whether it was equal. Well, they cared only about the Croats. They didn't care about the Serbs at all. It was 100 percent different, so it's not that there was some difference but a total difference. For example, the Serbs from Western Slavonia, they were supposed to leave their temporary homes in Croatia and go somewhere, and none of them knew what to tell them, where they should go, because the Croats were supposed to return and they could have only gone to the moon because their houses had been burned. So in response to your question, my answer is that they did not take care of the Serbs adequately, as they did of Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In these talks, did you hear perhaps that they had a plan, that they were preparing some plan for the return of these refugees, and especially referring to refugees from Western Slavonia? I'm actually asking about their return to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this was not a question at all. According to these negotiators and high officials of the UN, they were not being treated as their problem or, in a way, as human beings. They were not interested in where they would. They were just interested in having the Croats return there. And sometimes I would angrily say where should they go? Into the Danube? Or as I said a moment ago, up to the moon? Because they couldn't go back to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember what they would answer to you if you would put that question or if somebody else raised that question?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember how I would put that question. Because I did not put it directly. I would make an introduction in order to explain. I said, We behave or, rather, the international community behaves towards the Serbs as if we were rebels. We are not being recognised as if we were some kind of savages, and Croatia is an internationally recognised state and a recognised member of the UN, and now the Serbs are being asked to resolve this problem and they say that they cannot resolve it with Croatia. And then I said, since Croatia is a member of the international community, that they should resolve it half with the Serbs and half with the Croats. So at least to the extent to which they resolves the problem with us, they should resolve it with the Croats too. And they said, No, no, no, you have to work this out, but we don't talk to Croatia about this. In a way, they didn't want to talk about the return of Serbs to Croatia at all, justifying it by not having the mandate to do that. But I think that they did have the mandate. In my view, from a human point of view and from a legal point of view, this could not have been resolved just in a one-sided way.
