utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to go back a bit to a question that has to do with your contacts with international representatives, again, in relation to some provisions of the Vance Plan, and that has to do with disarmament. You remember that, according to the Vance Plan, disarmament was envisaged, inter alia. So this is what I'm interested in. In your contacts with international representatives, did they insist on having this disarmament carried out, regardless of these attacks that had already been referred to at the Miljavac plateau, Maslenica, the Medak pocket, and so on?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first they insisted on having this implemented 100 per cent, and we did hand over the heavy weaponry under this so-called double key. When Croatia carried out attacks, then these weapons were taken for us to defend ourselves. So for this month or two while the fighting went on, they didn't complain. But then again they insisted on having these weapons returned, although they did not guarantee security. And, of course, they couldn't when it was established on the ground that they had not been providing it in the first place. We had a double problem. That is to say, this constant fear of a Croat attack, then the UN, the -- they promised to protect us, did not protect us, and our soldiers were on the border protecting the territory. They didn't know where Croatia would attack. And, on the ground, there weren't any law enforcement forces so we had to face crime because we could not control everything on both sides. We had a limited number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just clarify this: You say that they insisted that these weapons should be returned after combat, after the end of combat. What did that mean "after the end of combat or fighting"? Can you tell us this a bit more precisely. What was meant by this "end of combat"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the incident at the Miljavac plateau, when we thought that there would be no other incidents, when the situation calmed down, they did not really ask us to do that while the fighting was still going on, the shooting was still going on. Their mortal was not at such a low level. But then afterwards they did ask that this be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And when the army of the Republic of Serb Krajina would get such weapons again, when did this actually take place? Was it after attacks or in some other situation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, they had to take this either if Croatia would secretly attack or if we would get information that Croatia would attack in a day or two. But I really have to tell you quite frankly that I did not deal with these military questions very precisely so I cannot speak about this under oath.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like us to touch upon another topic that was also highlighted by the Prosecutor during the cross-examination. This has to do with Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. One of the assertions put forth by the Prosecutor was that Arkan was your security. I'm going to read out that question to you. It is on page 9945. It reads as follows: [In English] "The fact is, Mr. Hadzic, that Arkan, in fact, did provide security for you on numerous occasions not only through 1991 but also 1992 and 1993. Isn't that true?" [Interpretation] You have provided an answer to that question but I would like us to clarify this a bit. To the best of your knowledge -- well, of course, perhaps you cannot be quite precise, but can you tell us in this period from 1991 to 1993, how many people did Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, have under his command?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have precise information. I couldn't count them. I just remember what he stated in public in the media on TV and some of the comments of my drivers and friends who were better informed than I was. That sometimes he would exaggerate this. So I think it was between 100 and 200, 250 men maximum. Usually around 100 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know roughly what kind of weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan and a few of these senior officers of his had Hecklers, Heckler/Koch rifles, very expensive ones. And the rest had the most up-to-date infantry weapons, automatic rifles, things like that. That's what I could see when I came to that centre. Every day I saw the guards there. In a way, they controlled this road that I had to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, arrive with a unit like that to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem in order to provide security for you? I'm referring to you personally.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course not. When he arrived, he probably didn't even know who I was. I certainly didn't know who he was. I never had a security detail of more than five or six men at one point in time, in a single day. I've already mentioned that. And I think I've already given the names of all of my body-guards from 1991 to 1993, and later on, from 1996 to 1997, because I reactivated most of them. So Zeljko Raznjatovic had a combat unit. It wasn't my understanding that he was anybody's private security. He came to fight with long-barrelled weapons. That's what I managed to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this period between 1991 and 1993 and perhaps even later, did you ever issue any orders, any instructions to Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Also as I moved about in the field, I did not see anyone who gave him any kind of orders. I really have no knowledge to that effect. I was never present at any one of their meetings, say, with Biorcevic or something like that. I could not see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1991, was it necessary for such a unit headed by him to come to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem to provide security for you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is completely wrong. I mean, even to ask something like that. Right now, in hindsight, I can tell Their Honours when I see all of that, what I know now, I couldn't -- I didn't need to have any kind of security because I was not incident-prone in any way. I did not have any -- I was not involved in any incidents. In 1991 I had this driver who was my body-guard too and he suggested that bringing in Japundzic because he said that he was not a good driver. And as they also said, we socialised more than we worked because there was really no need for them to protect me. I have never heard from anyone, except for Arkan and Badza, that I was in any kind of danger. I didn't even hear that from the Croats. They were just talking. They were saying, You have poor security, et cetera, et cetera. However, in 1991, I never reenforced my security detail. I just stayed on with these two men.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the same page, the Prosecutor, amongst other things, suggested that you socialised with him quite a lot in order to improve your position in the authorities, and he also promised that he would intimidate others on your behalf. Please, was there any need of that kind in 1991? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct. This is completely distorted. I believe that the opposite was true. I had already become president when I still didn't know him. When he turned up, he was a hindrance more than anything else. He was incident-prone and he was not very well loved by the Serbs in Pacetin, Bobanje [phoen], Trpinja whom I talked to. I'm not saying that he went against my authority but he certainly never improved it. I never worked with him. I only saw him from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, Your Honour, just to say that -- I don't know that we would agree with the characterisation of what was put to Mr. Hadzic on his cross, whether there's a record reference that Mr. Zivanovic can give us. I don't know that it was suggested by the Prosecution that Hadzic socialised with Arkan in order to improve his position. I think the word that was put to Mr. Hadzic on the cross was that he associated with Arkan, which has a different meaning. I could be wrong. If counsel could direct me to the transcript where I said "socialised," then I would stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't read that portion of transcript and maybe it was my -- my interpretation, but I'll do it now. It is the same transcript page, 9945. It is from line 6: "You associated yourself with him frequently. Did you it -- you did this because it enhanced your own powers and enable you to intimidate others and to get your way by associating yourself with Zeljko Raznjatovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell us whether your previous answer actually covers what I've just read out to you or is there anything you wish to add?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It suffices. I would say that the opposite was true. There was no intimidation at all. You will certainly understand from the witnesses that I never intimidated somebody. So just the opposite was true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us whether you met with him by arranging those meetings or did he arrange those meetings or was there anything else involved?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that I ever looked for him, perhaps a couple of times only. The -- one of those times was when I had problems with Klis [phoen] and then I went to the centre. I would also -- always meet him either on the road, in town, in the village. When I was somewhere, he would follow me. At first I thought that those were chance meetings but then I started suspecting that he was actually really following me. He mostly came to Erdut to the courtyard of the government building. He just turned up. I never called him. I never invited him. And then when he threatened me about the Vance Plan, I actually realised -- I was certain that he was following me. Actually, it was a threat against Babic, and then I realised that it was addressed at me as well, when he said to Babic that he would kill his children and I don't know what. But I have to be honest and say that he never threatened me personally and directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When we are talking about the security detail provided to you by Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, the Prosecutor also asked you about his presence in Velepromet on the 29th November, 1991. I'm going to read that transcript page. It's 9957: [In English] "Isn't it true that he provided security for you to get from Erdut to the Velepromet facility in Vukovar on the 20th of November 1991? "A. That is not true. He did not provide security for my route to Erdut in 1991, 1992 or 1993." [Interpretation] And later on page 9958, the next page, you were shown a portion of your interview with the investigator Dzuro. I'm talking about the part about Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, going to Velepromet and why he did that. And your answer is on page 9958 and I quote: [In English] "We needed that. It's not that we had to penetrate through the area but we didn't want any incidents to occur in Vukovar because Arkan had sufficient authority in order to prevent this kind of incident." [Interpretation] I'm sure you remember this part of the examination.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. But the interpretation I received - and that may be due to the differences between Croatian and Serbian - that Arkan had competencies. I said "authority." If it is one and the same, then it's okay. He was not authorised but he had his own personal power. I believe that's what I said. He was not officially authorised to do anything, and I think it's a very big difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that you used the word "authority." And that's what I see in the original text as well. However, I just wanted to ask you what you meant when you said "we needed that"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apologise for the interruption Your Honour. Just to say that I believe counsel's referring to the suspect interview with Mr. Dzuro and, in fact, here Mr. Hadzic's prior statement as from his testimony in the Dokmanovic case, not from his suspect interview. So, just for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. It was my error.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me just correct something -- yes, that is your prior testimony, the Dokmanovic case. I misspoke when I quoted the source. Let me repeat the question. As a matter of fact, what did you want to say when you said "we needed that"?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I used the personal pronoun "we," I meant the government. What I meant was that the government needed to prevent any possible incidents in Velepromet because some members of the government were afraid and didn't even dare to go to Vukovar. I said I will go at any cost. I have nothing to fear. They requested additional guarantees - Dr. Hadzic particularly - and that's why they invited Arkan to provide security for the entire government. And the conflation started from there. That was the beginning of the rumours that Arkan was my security detail, and then the JNA and everybody else exploited that. And it was a good enough reason for them to cover up Arkan's role and mask his order givers. They actually masked his role under the pretense that he was my security detail, but he wasn't. That's simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, I'm going to read yet another part of the Prosecutor's questions and your answers. I don't believe that you will have the time to answer my question. I will read first and then during the break, you can actually think about the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm quoting from page 9966: [In English] "And in what capacity then is he standing next to you? What's the reason why he's there with you at this press conference in Erdut? "A. It's difficult for me to answer now, considering that Arkan is dead and I don't know. I'm not sure whether he was standing there already when I started giving the interview, or he came later and stopped there in order to be in the picture. "Q. So could it be one of those occasions you've described where he was just trying to get close to you or was attempted to follow you around to get close to you? "A. That's the way it always happened. This is just one more such situation."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see the -- it is appropriate time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I heard your point about allowing him time to think about it, but is it something that requires a -- is it a question that he couldn't answer at this point? We could take the break, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, we could take the break. Because there are many questions after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Very well. So we take the break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, I believe that you still remember my question, i.e., that you remember the quote which was Mr. Stringer's question. Amongst other things, let me remind you of what you said in your answer. You said that you didn't know whether he was standing next to you only to be in the photo. My question is this: According to you, did Arkan like publicity?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of his main features. That's why he tried to engage the journalist van Lynden to be his private journalist. However, I remembered something else about that interview. When the Prosecutor showed me that, the journalist asked me about the visit of the mayor of Belgrade. When Mr. Unkovic was there, I wasn't with him. I was prevented from hosting him. However, I saw in the photo that somebody received him on behalf of the government. I believe it was Dr. Hadzic and I also saw Arkan. And I remember that in a way. Arkan was his host because they had known each other from Belgrade. I suppose that he stood next to me because he expected that the journalist would ask him about the visit. He was always on TV, every day, so his photo could have been taken even without me in it, but I suppose that he expected that he would be asked about the visit because Unkovic visited him as well, as far as I can remember. So I believe that explains the whole situation. Maybe it would be interesting to learn something about my security detail. I didn't tell you either but maybe the Trial Chamber would like to know when I lost in the election, Martic sent the police to confiscate my car since they couldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Hadzic. Apologies for the interruption. Your Honour, I'm look at Rule 90 on testimony of witnesses. 90(F) says that the Trial Chamber shall exercise control over the mode and order or interrogating witnesses and presenting evidence so as to make the integration and presentation effective for the ascertainment of the truth and avoid needless consumption of time. And I would respectively suggest, Your Honour, that much of what we've heard so far in this redirect is actually just a rehash, sort of just a restating of the direct examination. I know counsel has referred to some questions that were put to Mr. Hadzic during cross but it's largely just saying again what was said before. And it's not true re-direct in that sense, in our submission, and just now where Mr. Hadzic is sort of taking the floor to provide some more information on an issue that was dealt with on the cross without really having been asked to is really taking a step further, so we object to the -- what we think is a needless consumption of time and not a proper form of re-direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, sorry, you were going to say something --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- in reply. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All my questions were put in order to clarify the question -- the answers the accused gave to the -- on the Prosecution's questions, and I quoted all the Prosecution questions, and all of these questions are closely related to the matters raised by the Prosecution in course of their cross-examination. And, as far as I see, Mr. Hadzic gave -- give -- gave his answers in a way he -- he -- he find it appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The observation that frames Mr. Stringer's objection is, of course, not a -- an uncommon problem in these proceedings, and in that vein, I would remind you, Mr. Zivanovic, that you should focus your question on the points that would have arisen in cross-examination which you would wish to have clarified for the benefit of such future submissions as you would make to the Trial Chamber. And, Mr. Hadzic, I would remind you that you should listen to the question and only answer the question asked. And the way a question is phrased should not be used as an opportunity to make -- to volunteer information that you -- you -- you want to somehow get in. So counsel on his feet is the one who is to guide this process, so, Mr. Zivanovic, I would ask you to keep your witness under control.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll do, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, I'm not sure about the previous question. You did begin, actually, to give an answer and gave it partially but then you were interrupted. What I'm interested in is whether you wanted to answer the question I already asked you, or if you wanted to say something else, if you wanted to answer my question, then please complete your answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Zivanovic, isn't that precisely -- isn't that precisely the problem that Mr. Stringer has put his finger on. It isn't for the witness to say something else if he wants. Question and answer, and only the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And -- and, Your Honour, I am not aware whether Mr. Hadzic completed his answer on my question. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Let's -- let's move forward quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted to say something about security, and I can tell you how it worked if you ask me that, because the Prosecutor asked me that too. I was asked whether Arkan was my security. I wanted to say that he didn't and to explain how I provided a security myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question would specifically be linked with the Prosecutor's assertion that Arkan was your security. Was there a need for him to provide security to you at Erdut during the meeting with Mayor Unkovic.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no need, at least 20 kilometres around there was no possibility of any enemy activities. So there was no need for him to secure me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And was it necessary for him to provide security for you during the interview with the TV journalist?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nor was he doing that. He was either just standing there so his photo would be taken or he was waiting in line to be interviewed next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the cross-examination, you were shown Exhibit P2715. It's tab 742.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 34 in English. And I would just like to look at it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's the penultimate paragraph. There is no need to include the B/C/S text as well. General Panic is speaking here and I will just read out to you the first sentence where he says: [In English] "He is a person who had some good contacts with the press, and press loved him for several reasons. He could speak several languages, and that's why the foreign press maintained contacts with him. He was a good host."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So my question is whether this is correct, what General Panic said on this occasion about Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He obviously had better information than me, but I think that it was true that he was on good terms with foreign journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apologies for the intervention. I don't recall showing this to Mr. Hadzic on cross-examination. I wonder if there's a reference for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think it was shown but not maybe this particular part of this document. Anyway, I'm not -- I'm not -- I'll not put any other questions related to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, the Prosecutor asked you also about a meeting you had with Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and the Dutch journalist van Lynden.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 9960.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You probably remember his testimony before the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I wanted to remind you of something from his statement and his testimony about this meeting at the patisserie to leave alone everything that happened later. Could you tell me whether what he said at the time is true -- or, rather, can you first tell me something about this meeting and communication, whether you personally took part in this conversation between the journalist, van Lynden, and Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan. Did you actively participate in it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't participate in it at all. I was just introduced to this man, and I was brought there by a trick. Because a friend I knew said, Let us meet at the patisserie and then ten or 15 minutes later Arkan showed up and said, Let me introduce you to a journalist. He is very important. He works for the CIA. I remember that very well. So we shook hands, and I may have been there for five minutes. When I heard that Arkan wanted some weapons from him and wanted him to follow Arkan around, film him, and make interviews with him for CNN or whatever other media companies, when I heard that, I just said goodbye and left. I didn't want to participate in that because I thought it was crazy for a journalist to be able to procure weapons and how could such things be?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please tell me if you remember how they talked, in what language?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They talked in English. And my level of knowledge was not very much at the time but I understood some parts of the conversation. Weapon and so on. And if he worked for the CIA how could he do it? No one would allow him to do it at the time and he requested a pair of some special pistols. But it was all nonsense. And van Lynden, of course, did not agree to that, nor could he have done it. I just went back and sat at the table with the company that I had arrived there with and I left soon afterwards, as soon as I had paid my bill.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And during the cross-examination, the Prosecutor also told you at one point -- he made an assertion that Arkan was the commander of the Serb Volunteer Guard. From what you knew, you confirmed that, as far as I remember?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 10.000, it's also stated that he continued commanding units of the Serbian Volunteer Guard in operations in the Republic of Serbian Krajina. From what you know, did Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, take part in combat operations in the first place and did he command any units?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if he personally participated, because as he was elected deputy in the assembly of the Republic of Serbia, he withdrew from the military operations, and I wasn't informed about his activities. I didn't ask him, nor was I on such terms with him, but I know from the media and from the conversations I had with Mile Novakovic that some of those so-called his men took part in fighting around Obrovac and in fighting on Velebit, and so on. But it wasn't Arkan. These were the men that were called his men, in a way, or those who were part of the Army of the Republic of the Serbian Krajina. I'm not sure what it was then. But some people did call them the Tigers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a document. If we could please look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's P1937, tab 803. It's on page 10.003. I think it's on page 2, if we can please have a look at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I will try to find it for you on this page, the B/C/S text, regarding your -- your contacts with Arkan. But it seems that -- yes. Yes. It's the second paragraph in English, and here -- I think that it's the second paragraph in the first column. Yes. Can you see it well now?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How does the text begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: "The former first man of the Republic of Serbian Krajina" --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says: "I was here with Arkan every day, bombs were exploding all around, if not for anything else then because of my personal courage and that's why Zeljko attended the government sessions [sic]." Could you tell us whether you really told this sentence to the lady who interviewed you at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say that this is the biggest lie and fantasy that anyone could have imagined and written, not that I ever said it. I never thought that. It's not true, not a single letter of it. No bombs ever exploded in my vicinity. Arkan was never there. I was never sitting together with him. It's probably her -- it's probably she who wrote that in Belgrade but I don't know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, during the war, were you in your house in Pacetin all the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to make a mistake now. During the war, perhaps only twice I was there briefly for five minutes to see my mom and dad. I could not have been there because the house did not have the right amenities. It didn't have a proper roof. Had a mortar shell fallen there, it would have killed everyone and we didn't even have a basement where we could hide. So it was not only that I was not there, even if I wanted to, I ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Although you've answered my next question in a way, I would like it to be on the record, nevertheless. Is this correct that Arkan sat with you in Pacetin every day, there, in front of your house, while shells were falling?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan never sat with me in front of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that he was at government meetings because he was brave? I think that's the way she put it here; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that is not correct, and this has nothing to do with anything. This is absolutely insane. It wasn't that brave people attended government sessions. Government members attended the sessions, and that is not an issue now, whether they're brave or not, and if Arkan would enter a government session, he would not be there as a member of the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the fifth page of the English translation here, it says, inter alia, that you said when things were the most difficult in Knin, the response to call-up was 8 per cent; is that correct? Was that faithfully transmitted?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, this was not recorded, this interview. It was a conversation. And the journalist took notes. As for this particular piece of information specifically, I think that after the Maslenica operation, Spanovic, Stojan said to me that the response to mobilisation in Knin was very poor and that it was very low, less than 10 per cent, this first call-up response. I don't know whether she got this information from me or from somebody else, but it's not that it's baseless. It's the first day of the attack on Maslenica. Later on, it increased. I mean, the response to mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the third page of this same document, it says that you said that you started growing a beard at the beginning of the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This is an erroneous conclusion on her part or maybe she heard it from somebody else. I don't remember these silly details usually, but I do remember when I started growing a moustache and when I started growing a beard. A moustache in 1981, when I was in the army; and a beard in the spring of 1990, after the second round of Croatian elections, that is to say, a year before the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There's another thing I wanted to ask you, and it's on page 4 of the English translation. It says that Seselj was an unwanted guest in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'd have to see the context. Could you please direct me to where it is in the Serbian version. I think it should be scrolled down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To the right or to the left a bit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could be. I think it's a bit --

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it now. Maybe we could zoom in on the left-hand column.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The first paragraph. Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that I had this bad clash with Mr. Seselj at the time and he was an unwanted guest as far as I was concerned and other people who supported me. However, I did not meet with him, and I did not know when it was that he came there. He never called me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 10.012, the Prosecutor asked you, inter alia, about a meeting in the Ministry of Defence of Serbia where the then-minister, General Simovic, was present, and you were present, and also Arkan and a person with the nickname Kum. You wanted to say something -- or, rather, you were interrupted as you were providing your answer. So I'd like to ask you to say what it was that you wanted to say on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to say that it was Simovic who invited me to come to this meeting in Belgrade. Now was it through the secretary, his secretary, or how that Vlade, our secretary. Arkan was there, and this other person was there, and I don't know what that person's name is. And I did not take part in this meeting. I didn't really say anything because I saw that it was really not a serious meeting at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think that you wanted to explain then how it was that this meeting took place, or maybe I'm mistaken.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember now. I think that my concentration is down a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's all right. I'm not going to insist on that question now. On page 10.008, I'd like to ask you to clarify a particular matter. I'm going to read it out to you, the question and the answer, and then you're going to say what this pertains to exactly: [In English] "Q. Continuing down a few lines you say that some people objected, that Arkan attended RSK government sessions. "A. I respected his knowledge of the military and thus he attended the sessions. "Q. Now, Mr. Hadzic, what this suggests here is that, in fact, Arkan attended assembly sessions of the RSK because you wanted him to do so, isn't that how it was, because of his military skill? "A. No, this is absolutely incorrect. I did not say that nor can that stand in any sensible way. In my interpretation, I heard Assembly but here it says government of the RSK. I was not a member of the government. I had no influence on the agenda. I didn't attend the meetings. I personally attended the government meetings maybe two or three times but when I attended, Arkan was not present, so I don't know. These are some conclusions by the journalists and it's not anything that I myself said." [Interpretation] My question: I see here that what is referred to is Arkan's presence at assembly sessions and government sessions. So I just wanted to see whether we could clarify the matter. Can you explain this to us, this answer of yours? Does it have to do with assembly sessions or government sessions or both?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought that it pertained to assembly sessions when Arkan could come on his own and sit there as a guest because nobody could expel him or anybody else, and once he attended as a member of parliament of the Republic of Serbia. And when I said that this is incredible and that it's silly, it's because somebody had said that he came as a military expert. He never discussed any such thing and nobody ever asked him for his views on anything and these bodies did not discuss military matters or make decisions on military matters. I never attended the government session when Arkan was present there, so I don't know. According to some subsequent information, I think he was there only once and I heard that here when Martic said in a video-clip that Arkan attended a government session and that they quarrelled. This is the government of the Krajina in Knin. That was my understanding, not the government of Slavonia and Baranja.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please explain the answer you've provided just now, the first sentence, actually: [In English] "I thought that it pertained to assembly sessions when Arkan could come on his own and sit there as a guest because nobody could expel him or anybody else and once ..." [Interpretation] What were you actually trying to say?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my experience and on the basis of what I know, when Arkan would walk into an assembly session he would just sit there. He'd walk in and sit there. Nobody had invited him but he'd just stay, and other people, in a way, they could walk in and sit there because nobody asked for identification and nobody was calling out names and saying who could attend and who could not attend. That is what I was trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a document, P1845. 25

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is tab 1282. Could we have page 69, please, of the B/C/S original, and page 73 in the English translation. Maybe we should start with the previous page of the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that at the bottom of the page where it starts? I mean, what Zivota Panic is saying. And he says Arkan carried out missions in this area very well. At one point he broke away but then they brought him back, and so on. However, he is doing Yugoslavia a disservice.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move to next page in original, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He should be called and given a task. Those who sent him there should call him. I do not know who sent him. However, Arkan was present in Bijeljina, Zvornik, around Sarajevo, Knin, et cetera. This is what I'm interested in now. You spoke here about going to Bijeljina in order to meet Fikret Abdic, but this is what I'm interested in too. Did you go to Zvornik when Arkan was there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I went nowhere. I went to none of these towns, except Bijeljina that is on the road between Knin and Vukovar. And I did not even know where Arkan was waging war and who he had agreed with. And I never met with him and I never had the opportunity of discussing these topics with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the next sentence it says: "Somebody is leading him and issuing tasks to him. We should see who this is. It is certain that it is not us." Can you tell us now since it was stated here that Arkan was part of your security. Did the members of your security go around Zvornik and Sarajevo even though you did not go there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't go anywhere without me. When they were free, they were at their homes, and they rested with their families. As for this route from Vukovar to Knin, I never went anywhere apart from that, and my security was never at any place where I did not go to. So he really has nothing to do with me, and he was not part of my security.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact -- I'm going to read one portion from this document which was shown to you by the Prosecutor and I'm also going to read the answer you provided. The page number is 10.041: [In English] "Mr. Hadzic, before the break, we were looking at P1845. "Mr. Stringer: And indeed the page of B/C/S that we wanted is page 62 of the document in B/C/S which is -- ends with the ERN number 4965. And towards the bottom, that's it. Thank you. Toward the bottom, I should say the bottom third, Panic is talking here about the expulsions in Lovas and that Lovas is constantly being watched by Jovic's Chetniks, the White Eagles. Now, Mr. Hadzic, Zivota Panic knew about this. It is your evidence that you didn't know anything about Mr. Jovic's activities and those of his White Eagles in Lovas during this period? "A. Yes, that's what I said that I didn't know anything about it. "Q. Well, in April of 1992, when this is happening, it was possible for you to go to this area, isn't it? You were able to move down through Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the Republic of Serbian Krajina at the time, and it was all free, and then in the next paragraph he says that we must have a serious showdown with Arkan and the White Eagles. He says Arkan is led by Hadzic." [Interpretation] Tell me, please -- as a matter of fact, I'm going to finish the quote so that I don't have to come back to it later: [In English] "Mr. Stringer: Could we have tab 459, please, Exhibit P1845, page 86 of the English; page 62, 63 of the B/C/S. "Q. Mr. Hadzic, this is the record of the SFRU Presidency held in April of 1992, the 16th, do you recall what Mr. Panic's position was at that time? "A. I think that he was the commander of the 1st Military District but I'm not 100 per cent sure about it. "Q. We can go back to page 2 of this. Indicates that as of that time of this meeting, he was the acting chief of the General Staff or Chief of the Main Staff of the JNA. Would you disagree with that? "A. I agree. I'm just a bit confused. I know that he was appointed a commander of the 1st Military District, but I don't know that he was appointed commander. "Q. Now moving to page 86 ..." [Interpretation] I'll stop here and invite you to provide an explanation at this point regarding what we see on the screen. General Panic, while saying that Arkan was in Bijeljina, Zvornik, around Sarajevo and in Knin said, Somebody is leading him. Somebody is giving him his tasks. You had the opportunity to hear at that same meeting that somebody said that you were actually leading him, that Arkan was led by Hadzic. Tell me, please, do you think that, in your view, while General Panic was speaking at that meeting was he sincere? Was he honest when he said that you were the one who was leading Arkan, or was he was sincere when he said that he didn't know who was leading Arkan and who gave him his task?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that he was sincere when he said it was me. But he was also not sincere when he said he didn't know who was it. Because before that, Panic says that Arkan carried out his task well which means that it was the JNA who led him. But then he realised that he made a mistake, that he put his foot in his mouth so he tried to reiterate so Arkan was led by the army, and the army were one and the same, so Panic lied because he was speaking before the Presidency, the highest body of Yugoslavia that appointed him. He lied, so he actually made up that it was me. But everybody understood that he was lying. I'm sure that everybody understood then and still understand now. I really didn't have anything to do with Arkan. I didn't have any information whatsoever about Arkan's work or who was behind that work. Obviously Panic knew that very well, but he did not want to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether you can conclude from the text or perhaps you know from some other sources what tasks did General Panic have in mind when he said that Arkan carried them out really efficiently?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only assume that Panic was satisfied with his activities in Slavonia and Baranja when he was a member of Biorcevic's corps. I can only assume that because I didn't hear anybody from the army attacking him but I never attended meetings with him on those issues. Nobody reported to me either orally or in written form about any of those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to either see or hear that some high-ranking officers said something good about the behaviour of Zeljko Raznjatovic, Arkan, and his unit?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have such opportunities. I saw it in the newspaper -- newspapers. General Biorcevic commended him, and also both him and Badza were rewarded with some trophy weapons. He moved in those circles in Belgrade among very influential people, that is. At that time I couldn't do that, nor did I have any opportunity to meet with anybody of those people and rub shoulders with them like Arkan did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, do you remember who awarded him with those trophy weapons in recognition of his work?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the commander of the Novi Sad Corps, Andrija Biorcevic, who did that. That was the same general who, after the liberation of Vukovar, was received by General Panic, who was the chief of the General Staff. He was the first next to him. Panic congratulated him on that occasion. He was one of Panic's closest associates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Amongst other things, I quoted a portion of a question relative to Jovic's Chetniks, White Eagles, to be more precise, what General Panic said about Lovas, Jovic, and all those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at the same document, page 67, in the original, and in English, it would be page 70. [In English] If we could scroll down English text, please. Oh. Maybe you should move to the next page in English. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is paragraph 1 in English, as well in the original. You'll find that in the first paragraph. This is what Borisav Jovic said. He said: "When it comes to the Eagles and Arkan, I believe that the military should arrest all of them pursuant to our order." Could you please tell me whether you remember what Borisav Jovic's position was at the time.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was the acting president of the Presidency of the SFRY, which means number one man of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command that you are talking about is the Supreme Command of the armed forces of the SFRY. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you did. At that time, it was still the JNA, but he was the number one man of its Supreme Command, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, in view of the time when this happened and in view of everything that I told you about General Panic's words and I even quoted from his discourse where he said that at one point you were the one who was leading Arkan. Were you at all informed about the requirement to arrest Arkan? Were you told that you should do something about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. At that time everybody knew that he was under the direct subordination and control of Belgrade and that he had nothing whatsoever to do with the Krajina Serbs, that he had arrived as a member of federal institutions. That's how he behaved. Nobody from Belgrade ever sent me either a verbal or a written report or complaint about his conduct in the area. I understand why they didn't, because everybody knew that I was not responsible for any of that. That's the most logical explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 21st of July, the Prosecutor showed you yet another document; it's P1878. He also showed you something. In order to avoid rephrasing, I'm going to read the question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we have, please, P1878, tab 531: "Q. Mr. Hadzic, while it's come up, this is the Supreme Defence Council of the FRU in July of 1992, about thee months after the meeting, the Presidency meeting, we were just talking about. Zivota Panic present there. And I would direct your attention to page 14 of the English, 16 of the B/C/S. And here now in July of 1992, Panic is saying: Many things have been said about Arkan. Measures had been taken. However, you should look for Goran Hadzic to find out what Arkan doing. He keeps him around as a body-guard and he leads him. And then in the next passage, Momir Bulatovic says essentially that Arkan is getting stronger again. That means someone was -- someone is behind these people. The question now, Mr. Hadzic, is again here in July of 1992, it is Zivota Panic who is correct, isn't it, that, in fact, if somebody wanted to know where Arkan was and what he was doing, they just should find you because Arkan was close to you as a body-guard?"

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will kindly ask you to look at the following page in the same document. We have not seen that page yet. In English, it's actually on the same page. You don't have to change the English page for the time being? Slobodan Milosevic also attended that meeting and he says -- the question was: "And he has units?" Slobodan Milosevic answers: "I don't think so. No, according to the information that I received from our ministry, he doesn't have any. Arkan was also a volunteer at the time when the army was operating on the battle-field and he was under the army command. He was not on his own." I'm going to ask you this: Do you think that Slobodan Milosevic who shared the information that he received, that he didn't have any other information.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he said at the end that he was under the control of the army, that's correct. And what he said before that, that he didn't have information, I don't think that he was telling the truth. I believe that Milosevic knew very well what Arkan was doing and who was behind Arkan. I believe that he had complete information, unlike me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain why General Panic again brought him in connection with you? Obviously you can explain if you know. Why did he put Arkan in that same context again and claim that he was your body-guard?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he was trying to deceive all those people at the meeting, if that was at all possible. Because everybody knew that he didn't have anything to do with me. On the previous page, Bulatovic said that he was driving around Herzegovina in a car with police registration plates. Everybody knew that this was a blatant lie, that Arkan enjoyed support from Belgrade. You can look at the following page of the Serbian text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It's on the previous page. However, in the English version, Bulatovic's words appear on the page that we have on the screen in the first line at the top of the page.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And let me just tell you that I was never in Herzegovina, not during the war, not before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a document, 1908; transcript page 1047. And on page 1049 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's correction: 10.049.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: He asked you a question that I will now read out to you. Reads -- he is actually quoting General Panic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Sorry, counsel. I believe this was led in private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, okay. Maybe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So should we go into private session for you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: -- put the question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes. Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic the interpretation was still ongoing from your last question, so I missed the last thing you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can repeat it in open session as well. I just said to Mr. Hadzic that I'll not show him this document that he mentioned because they are already in evidence and they were not subject of the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I thought you had said something after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, after that nothing. Yeah, I just said that it is time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take the adjournment until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
